title: Three clearing-house permissions put different risks before the Bank
summary: A clearing house wanting to withhold information, outsource an important activity or link its clearing service to another venue would face three separate tests under the Bank’s proposed rulebook. The November statement explains what evidence the Bank expects in each case and how it could condition, vary or revoke a permission. The distinction matters to clearing members. A disclosure permission changes the information available to them. Outsourcing changes who performs a service while leaving the CCP responsible. Interoperability can connect exposures and financial resources across two operators. Approval of one arrangement gives a member no assurance that another has been approved.

For disclosure, the CCP must identify the information and explain how publication would threaten its business secrets or its safety and soundness. If it proposes an altered disclosure, it should show how that form addresses the risk. A request to withhold the information altogether should explain why modification will not work. The Bank can attach conditions, including a requirement to disclose information differently. It expects to determine applications generally within 30 business days, or within 90 business days for a complete application in exceptional circumstances. Reduced public detail can therefore be consistent with an authorised arrangement, but the case for withholding has to be made explicitly.

The outsourcing application concerns major activities linked to risk management. The Bank asks for the proposed written agreement and the evidence behind the decision, including the division of responsibilities, access to information and risks from further outsourcing. A board remains accountable for compliance even if specialist staff and systems sit with a provider. The Bank can examine the transition and impose conditions or intermediate checkpoints. The normal expected decision time is 80 business days. In exceptional circumstances the statement gives six months from receipt of a complete application. A service provider’s proposed start date and the regulator’s approval are separate inputs to a launch plan.

A new interoperability agreement, or a material change to an existing one, requires another application. A short commercial description is insufficient. The package includes the trades proposed for clearing, their contractual terms, trading or registration sources, pricing inputs and the evidence for any proxies. The operator must explain the risks created by the link and demonstrate compliance with the relevant rules. For a member, the quality of prices used in margin and stressed-loss calculations can matter as much as the convenience of connecting two venues. The normal and exceptional assessment periods follow the 80-business-day and six-month pattern for this permission.

The publication describes decisions and supervisory expectations, not the performance of an actual arrangement. The Bank intends to explain refusals or conditions and generally to publish details of approvals, subject to exceptions where disclosure would be inappropriate or unnecessary. A member planning to use a linked service should seek the scope and conditions of the written permission. An absence of detail in the public record cannot establish the terms of an outsourcing contract, the quality of prices or how losses would reach the member if the link were stressed.

questions.question: If the CCP withholds information, what can a member still use to evaluate its exposure?
questions.detail: The proposed policy allows modified disclosure and requires the operator to justify why complete withholding is necessary. The published record may therefore leave a gap even where the Bank has examined the issue. Obtain the wording and conditions of the permission and the substitute information the operator makes available. Test whether it lets a member monitor a specific risk or would require additional contractual reporting.

questions.question: Could the CCP maintain oversight if a material provider changed its own suppliers?
questions.detail: The Bank asks about access, responsibilities and further outsourcing, while the CCP board remains accountable. That distinction matters to a participant depending on timely risk calculations. Review the proposed agreement, rights to information, transition checkpoints and evidence that the CCP can act if service deteriorates. Assess the practical dependencies across the provider chain rather than relying solely on the first provider’s service commitment.

questions.question: How would the two clearing houses value an exposure when one market price becomes unreliable?
questions.detail: The interoperability application requires price sources and explanations of proxies. A member can face changed margin needs even if no trade has defaulted. Compare the contractual products and pricing records with the two operators’ margin and stress methods. Examine how disagreement is resolved under the arrangement and how any additional collateral requirement would reach a clearing member in time to fund it.

limitation: The permissions are described in a near-final statement. Individual determinations, conditions and exceptional timeframes depend on the application.
